prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form that made incretin-based treatment of diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: B027 remains the only candidate with a complete arc from hormone biology to medicine: proglucagon processing, the bioactive GLP-1(7-36) peptide, human physiology of secretion and action, receptor biology and the therapeutic concept, then drugs with more than two decades of independent confirmation and randomized outcome evidence in glycaemia, weight, and cardiovascular and renal endpoints. Round 1 showed that no member disputes the science or its maturity; the open questions are the third name and the citation wording. I hold a single prize part with Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, and I read the citation as honouring the physiology and the identification of the active peptide, with the medicines as the consequence rather than the object of the prize. A single part keeps the credit clean and avoids diluting a three-person cap.
statement.case_against: The attribution remains the weakness. Habener is not on the credited list, Mojsov's priority for the active peptide is contested, and Knudsen's acylated analogues are what reached patients at scale. I still cannot settle priority from the supplied material, and I would not claim to. If the committee concluded from documents that Mojsov's contribution is not independent and prior enough, the right fallback is Drucker and Holst or Drucker, Holst and Knudsen, not a hurried reshuffle. A discovery-side citation may also be read as honouring the idea but not the drug, and that criticism has force.

responses.point: Linnarsson argues that Knudsen's design of acylated long-acting analogues solved the half-life problem and was itself a discovery, and that Mojsov is the most contested name.
responses.response: I have reconsidered this and I accept that the half-life solution is a real scientific step, not only engineering. It does not change my configuration, because it answers a different question from the one the citation asks. If the prize honours the physiology and the active peptide, Mojsov belongs, and Knudsen's work builds on that target. Contested priority is a reason to review the record, not a negative finding in itself. I do concede that your configuration is the better one if the committee decides the prize is for the physiology-to-medicine arc, and that this is the decision that should settle the third name, not a count of how many members prefer Mojsov.

responses.point: Perlmann proposes Drucker and Holst as a two-name fallback if documentary evidence on the peptide identification is unclear, and treats analogue development as industry work built on earlier foundations.
responses.response: I agree the two-name fallback is the right shape if the priority question cannot be resolved, since Drucker and Holst are named by all six of us and no one disputes them. I would trigger it only on a documented finding that Mojsov's work was not independent or not prior, not on the existence of a dispute. Where I part from you is the view that industrial development sits outside the prize. Knudsen's contribution is substantial, and I would exclude it on the grounds of what the citation honours and the three-name limit, not because industry work cannot be a discovery.

responses.point: Svenningsson, as chair, asks whether Habener's absence undermines any GLP-1 configuration and whether the priority question must be resolved before voting.
responses.response: I made a settled priority review a condition of my support in round 1 and I keep that condition, but I would state it plainly: the committee cannot resolve it from the supplied names, and none of us has offered documents rather than recollection. So I treat it as a stated uncertainty that my vote carries. Habener's absence is a real limit on any configuration with a credit list this size. It argues for careful citation wording, which says the physiology of GLP-1 and its active form, rather than for dropping the candidate. I also now follow your point that the wording should say clearly what is being honoured, so I keep the active form in the text.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius keeps the prize anchored in physiology, notes long-term safety beyond metabolic disease is still being defined, and holds CAR-T and TNF blockade as alternatives if GLP-1 attribution stalls.
responses.response: I agree with the physiology anchor and I take the safety point as a reason to keep the citation to demonstrated effects. I do not think the unresolved safety questions in new indications weigh against recognition, since the diabetes, obesity and outcome-trial evidence is established. On your alternatives, I have dropped CAR-T from mine because the missing upstream credit for the first chimeric receptors is a gap I cannot close with three names. If GLP-1 attribution stalled, I would turn to a cleaner two-name basic-science candidate before a clinical-translation one.

responses.point: El-Manira holds optogenetics (B015) and the unfolded protein response (B014) as alternatives, and notes that Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenboeck have claims that a three-name cap cannot absorb.
responses.response: I agree on B015, and the chair's questions made me weigh it harder. Nagel and Hegemann's channelrhodopsin and Deisseroth's neuronal adaptation are separable steps, and a fair trio still leaves out Bamberg, Boyden or Miesenboeck. I keep it as an alternative but rank it below B014 on credit, since Mori and Walter give the cleanest two-name attribution on the shortlist and about thirty years of independent confirmation. Your point that B014 may be held back by indirect medical impact is fair, but that affects whether it should be the main prize, not whether it makes a good alternative.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for GLP-1(7-36) against Habener and others is documented well enough to credit her, which I cannot judge from the supplied material.
Whether the committee intends to honour the physiology and active peptide or the physiology-to-medicine arc with analogue design, which determines Mojsov versus Knudsen.
Whether B015 can be given a defensible three-name credit without excluding Bamberg, Boyden or Miesenboeck.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for any credited name in B027, B014 or B015. I have eight co-authored works with Sten Linnarsson and have worked with Jonas Frisen, none of whom is credited and none of that work concerns the shortlisted discoveries. I note topical proximity to the SMN2 splicing candidate (B016) because of my RNA-processing work, and I have not made it a preferred or alternative choice. Shared Karolinska affiliation with colleagues is not a documented tie to any candidate.
